passages.happening:
The high priest asks, “Are these charges true?” (verse 1). Stephen answers with the story of his people. “Brothers and fathers, listen to me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran” (verse 2), and told him to leave his country for a land God would show him.

Abraham settled in Haran, and after his father died God brought him into this land. But God gave him “no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground” (verse 5), only a promise for his descendants, when he had no child. God told him his descendants would be foreigners, enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years, and then God would judge that nation and they would come out and worship him “in this place” (verse 7).

God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and Abraham became the father of Isaac, Isaac of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Stephen is on trial for speaking against the temple and the law. Instead of a short defence, he tells Israel's story from the beginning. His hearers knew this story by heart. What would have caught their attention is what he chooses to stress.

The first thing he stresses is where God appeared. ‘The God of glory’ met Abraham in Mesopotamia, far from the holy land and long before there was a temple. God was not tied to one place.

The second is that Abraham never owned the land. He lived in it as a guest, trusting a promise. Stephen calls Abraham ‘our father’, and he calls the council ‘brothers and fathers’. He is speaking as a Jew to Jews, about their shared ancestor.

Notice ‘worship Me in this place’ (verse 7). Stephen is accused of speaking against ‘this holy place’ (6:13). He shows that God's promise of worship ‘in this place’ came in a speech that began in a foreign land.
passages.ot:
Stephen retells Genesis 12 to 17. God's call: “Leave your country, your kindred, and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you” (Genesis 12:1). God's promise: “your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not their own, and they will be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years” (Genesis 15:13). The covenant of circumcision is in Genesis 17.

Genesis tells the call after the family had reached Haran (Genesis 12:1-4). But Genesis also has God say he brought Abraham “out of Ur of the Chaldeans” (Genesis 15:7), and Nehemiah says the same (Nehemiah 9:7). Stephen follows that thread and places the first call in Mesopotamia, where Ur lay.
passages.hard: Stephen says Abraham left Haran ‘after his father died’ (verse 4). By the numbers in Genesis, Terah was 70 when his sons were born (Genesis 11:26), Abraham left Haran at 75 (Genesis 12:4), and Terah died at 205 (Genesis 11:32), which would put Terah's death some sixty years after Abraham left. Readers answer this in different ways. Many note that Genesis 11:26 may name Abraham first because he matters most, not because he was the eldest, so he may have been born later. Others think Stephen followed a way of telling the story known in his day. These notes do not settle it; it does not touch Stephen's point.
passages.asks: Stephen's first point is that God met Abraham before there was a temple, a land or a nation, and Abraham trusted a promise he did not see fulfilled. Ask where you expect to meet God, and whether you have limited him to certain places. And ask whether you can live, as Abraham did, on a promise.

passages.happening:
“Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him” (verse 9). God rescued him, gave him wisdom before Pharaoh, and made him ruler over Egypt.

A famine came. Jacob sent his sons to Egypt for grain. On their second visit Joseph made himself known to them, and he sent for his father and all his relatives, “seventy-five in all” (verse 14). Jacob and the fathers died in Egypt. “Their bones were carried back to Shechem and placed in the tomb that Abraham had bought from the sons of Hamor at Shechem for a price he paid in silver” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Here is Stephen's second thread. Joseph was rejected by his own brothers, the fathers of Israel's tribes. But God was with him, even in Egypt, and the brother they sold became their rescuer. They did not know him on their first visit. They recognized him on the second.

The first hearers would not miss the likeness. The leaders of Israel had rejected Jesus. Stephen is telling them that this has happened before, in their own family, and that the rejected one was God's chosen deliverer.

And again God is at work outside the land. ‘God was with him’ in Egypt.
passages.ot: The story is told in Genesis 37 to 50. The family's number is given in Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5. The burial places are in Genesis 23 (Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah near Hebron from Ephron), Genesis 33:19 (Jacob buys land at Shechem “from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father”), Genesis 50:13 (Jacob is buried at Machpelah), and Joshua 24:32 (Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem).
passages.hard:
Two details here differ from Genesis, and honest readers have always noticed them.

The number. Genesis says seventy. Stephen says “seventy-five in all” (verse 14). The two numbers come from two forms of the Old Testament. The Hebrew text of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 says seventy. The Septuagint, the old Greek translation made before the time of Jesus, says seventy-five in Genesis 46:27, adding more descendants of Joseph's sons. Stephen was speaking in a Greek-speaking setting, and his number follows that Greek form of the text. Neither number is a head count of everyone who travelled; wives and servants are left out. The note on Genesis 46 says more.

The tomb. Stephen says the bones were laid ‘in the tomb that Abraham had bought from the sons of Hamor at Shechem’. In Genesis, Abraham bought a cave at Machpelah near Hebron from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23), and it was Jacob who bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19). Readers account for this in several ways. Many think Stephen is summing up two purchases, and two burial places, in one sentence, as people do when retelling a long story to make a point. Some suggest that Abraham, who built an altar at Shechem (Genesis 12:6-7), may also have bought ground there, though Genesis does not say so. Others think Stephen, speaking under pressure, joined the stories in a way a careful writer would not, and that Luke faithfully recorded what he said. Still others simply count it an error in the account.

These notes do not settle it. None of these details touches Stephen's argument, which is about God's faithfulness outside the land and Israel's habit of rejecting the deliverers God sent.
passages.asks: Joseph's brothers sold him and later bowed before him, and he forgave them. Ask whether there is someone you have pushed aside who may turn out to be God's gift to you. And notice that God was with Joseph in the place of his slavery. No place is too far from God.

passages.t: Moses: born, raised, and pushed away
passages.happening:
As the time of God's promise came near, the people grew in Egypt. A king who knew nothing of Joseph oppressed them and forced them to abandon their babies.

Moses was born then, “beautiful in the sight of God” (verse 20). When he was put outside, Pharaoh's daughter brought him up as her own son. “So Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful in speech and action” (verse 22).

At forty he went to visit his people. He saw one of them mistreated and struck down the Egyptian. “He assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him to deliver them, but they did not” (verse 25). The next day he tried to make peace between two Israelites, and one pushed him aside: “Who made you ruler and judge over us?” (verse 27). Moses fled to Midian and lived there as a foreigner.
passages.hearers:
Stephen was accused of speaking against Moses. Here he speaks of Moses with honour: beautiful to God, wise, powerful in word and deed, sent to deliver.

But the thread runs on. Moses came to save his people, and ‘they did not understand’. One of them pushed him away with the question that rings through the speech: ‘Who made you ruler and judge over us?’ The deliverer was rejected by the very people he came to help.

Stephen adds details Exodus does not give: that Moses was forty, and that he was educated in all the wisdom of Egypt. Exodus itself says only that he grew up in Pharaoh's household as the daughter's son (Exodus 2:10).
passages.ot: Stephen follows Exodus 1 and 2. Moses' mother saw “that he was a beautiful child” and hid him for three months (Exodus 2:2). Moses struck down an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew (Exodus 2:11-12). The next day one Israelite said to him, “Who made you ruler and judge over us? Are you planning to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?” (Exodus 2:14). Then Moses fled.
passages.asks: Moses thought his people would understand, and they did not. Ask whether you have been slow to recognize someone God was using to help you, because he came in a way you did not expect. Israel's story, Stephen says, is full of such moments.

passages.happening:
After forty years, an angel appeared to Moses in the flames of a burning bush in the desert near Mount Sinai. The Lord spoke: “I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (verse 32). “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground” (verse 33). God had seen his people's suffering and was sending Moses to Egypt.

“This Moses, whom they had rejected with the words, ‘Who made you ruler and judge?’ is the one whom God sent to be their ruler and redeemer” (verse 35). He led them out with wonders and signs. And this is the Moses who said, “God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers” (verse 37). He was with the people in the wilderness and “received living words to pass on to us” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Again the place is striking. The ‘holy ground’ is in the desert, near Sinai, outside the promised land. God made a place holy by being there.

Stephen's words ‘this Moses’ come again and again, like a hammer. This Moses, rejected; this Moses, sent; this Moses, who promised a prophet like himself. Stephen's hearers would know where the argument was going. Peter had already said that Jesus is the prophet like Moses (3:22).

Notice also how Stephen speaks of the law: ‘living words’. The man accused of speaking against the law calls it living words from God.
passages.ot: The burning bush is in Exodus 3. God told Moses, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). The promise of a prophet is from Deuteronomy: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers” (Deuteronomy 18:15).
passages.asks: God made a desert bush into holy ground and a rejected exile into a redeemer. Ask where God has met you that you did not expect, and whether you have dismissed someone God may have sent. And notice Stephen's love for the law: ‘living words’. Ask whether God's word is living for you, or only old.

passages.happening:
“But our fathers refused to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt” (verse 39). They told Aaron, “Make us gods who will go before us” (verse 40), made a calf and rejoiced in the work of their hands.

So God gave them over to worship the stars, as the prophets wrote: “Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?” They carried the shrine of Molech and the star of the god Rephan, idols they made. “Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Babylon” (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
Stephen's speech now turns sharper. He has shown God's faithfulness. Now he shows the people's unfaithfulness. They had Moses, the living words and God's presence, and still they turned back to Egypt in their hearts and made a god they could see.

Notice the phrase ‘the works of their hands’. It is the key to what comes next. Stephen will soon say that God does not dwell in houses ‘made by human hands’. To the first hearers, ‘made with hands’ was the language used of idols.

Stephen says ‘our fathers’. He includes himself in Israel's story, its glory and its failures alike. This is the way Israel's prophets spoke.
passages.ot:
The golden calf is in Exodus 32: “Come, make us gods who will go before us” (Exodus 32:1).

The quotation is from Amos 5:25-27. In the Hebrew, as in our Bibles, Amos names gods called Sakkuth and Kaiwan, and ends “I will send you into exile beyond Damascus” (Amos 5:27). Stephen follows the old Greek translation, which reads the names as Molech and Rephan. He also says ‘beyond Babylon’ instead of ‘beyond Damascus’. Amos spoke to the northern kingdom, which was taken away by Assyria, beyond Damascus. Stephen widens it to the later exile of Judah to Babylon, which his hearers knew well.
passages.asks: They wanted gods they could see and carry, and they ended up worshipping the works of their own hands. Ask what you are tempted to trust because you can see it and control it: money, a reputation, even a building. Stephen's warning is that good things can become idols.

passages.happening:
“Our fathers had the tabernacle of the Testimony with them in the wilderness” (verse 44), made just as God had shown Moses. It came into the land with Joshua and stayed until the time of David, who found favour with God and asked to build a dwelling for him. “But it was Solomon who built the house for Him” (verse 47).

“However, the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands” (verse 48). As the prophet says: “Heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me, says the Lord, or where will My place of repose be? Has not My hand made all these things?” (verses 49-50).
passages.hearers:
This is the heart of Stephen's reply to the charge against the temple. He does not say the temple was wrong. God commanded the tabernacle, and Solomon built the house. But God never lived in a box. The tabernacle was a tent that moved with the people. The temple was a gift, but heaven is God's throne.

‘Made by human hands’ was a strong phrase. Jews used it for idols. Stephen does not call the temple an idol, but he warns against treating it as if it held God, as if God could be owned or controlled by those who kept his house.

This was not a new idea. Solomon himself had said it on the day he opened the temple. And Jesus had spoken of a temple ‘not made with hands’ (Mark 14:58).
passages.ot:
Solomon prayed at the dedication of the temple, “But will God indeed dwell upon the earth? Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built” (1 Kings 8:27).

Stephen quotes Isaiah 66:1-2: “Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me?” Isaiah goes on: “This is the one I will esteem: he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word” (Isaiah 66:2). God looks for a humble heart more than a building.
passages.asks: Stephen loved the temple's God more than the temple. Ask whether you treat a building, a style of worship or a tradition as if it held God. God is glad to meet his people in a place, but he cannot be kept in one. He looks for those who tremble at his word.

passages.happening:
Then Stephen turns to his judges. “You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did” (verse 51).

“Which of the prophets did your fathers fail to persecute? They even killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One” (verse 52). And now, he says, they have betrayed and murdered him: they who “received the law ordained by angels, yet have not kept it” (verse 53).
passages.hearers:
‘Stiff-necked’ is a picture from farming: an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke. ‘Uncircumcised hearts and ears’ means hearts and ears closed to God, whatever the body bears. These are not Stephen's own insults. They are the words of the Law and the Prophets about Israel. God himself called his people ‘stiff-necked’ at Sinai.

So Stephen speaks as Israel's prophets had always spoken: from inside Israel, to Israel, in Israel's own words. Moses, Jeremiah and the others said the same hard things to their own people, because they loved them and wanted them to turn. Stephen's charge is aimed at the council in front of him, who had handed Jesus over, and he names them as heirs of those who killed the prophets.

‘The Righteous One’ is Jesus. ‘The law ordained by angels’ reflects a Jewish belief, found also in Paul's letters (Galatians 3:19) and in Hebrews (Hebrews 2:2), that angels had a part in the giving of the law at Sinai. Stephen's point is that the council, so proud of the law, has not kept it.
passages.ot:
The words come straight from Scripture. God said to Moses, “You are a stiff-necked people” (Exodus 33:5). Moses told Israel, “Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more” (Deuteronomy 10:16). Jeremiah said of his own people that “they stiffened their necks and did more evil than their fathers” (Jeremiah 7:26), and that “their ears are closed, so they cannot hear” (Jeremiah 6:10).

The killing of the prophets is confessed in Israel's own prayers: “They killed Your prophets, who had admonished them to return to You” (Nehemiah 9:26). One prophet, Zechariah son of Jehoiada, was stoned in the temple courtyard (2 Chronicles 24:21).
passages.hard:
Is Stephen condemning the Jewish people? No. He is a Jew speaking to the council of his own people, in the words of his own Scriptures, like Moses and Jeremiah before him. A prophet's rebuke from inside Israel is not a verdict on Jews. Stephen's own last words will be a prayer for forgiveness for the very men who kill him.

Sadly, Christians later lifted words like these out of their setting and used them against Jewish people, and the note on 2:22-28 tells how verses like these were misused and why this site rejects that reading. Read in its place, Stephen's speech is a family argument about what God was doing, spoken by a man who called his hearers ‘brothers and fathers’.
passages.asks: Stephen said what the prophets had said: that God's people can resist God while being sure they serve him. Ask whether that could be true of you, or of your church. The warning is not for ‘them’. It is for anyone who has the Scriptures and does not listen.

passages.t: Stephen sees Jesus, and is stoned
passages.happening:
The council members are enraged and gnash their teeth at him. “But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (verse 55). “Look,” he says, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (verse 56).

They cover their ears, shout, and rush at him together. They drag him out of the city and begin to stone him. “Meanwhile the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul” (verse 58).

As they stone him, Stephen prays, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (verse 59). Falling on his knees, he cries out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” “And when he had said this, he fell asleep” (verse 60).
passages.hearers:
Stephen speaks of ‘the Son of Man’ at God's right hand. In the Gospels this is almost always Jesus' own name for himself. Here a disciple uses it of the risen Jesus. To the council it was the claim Jesus had made at his own trial, and they had called it blasphemy then. Covering their ears was a way of refusing to hear what they took as blasphemy.

Jesus is usually pictured sitting at God's right hand. Here he is standing. Readers have suggested different reasons: that he rises to welcome his servant, or stands as a witness to speak for Stephen in heaven's court, as Stephen has spoken for him on earth. Luke does not explain, and more than one may be true.

The Law said that a blasphemer should be stoned outside the camp, and that the witnesses should throw the first stones. That is probably why the witnesses take off their outer cloaks. How the council could put Stephen to death is debated, since Jewish leaders had told Pilate they were not allowed to execute anyone (John 18:31). Many think the hearing broke down into a mob killing, since Luke tells of no sentence. Others suggest it happened when Roman control was weak; Pilate was removed from office in AD 36, but the date of Stephen's death is not known.

And then Luke names a young man: Saul. The church's fiercest enemy is introduced at the death of its first martyr, holding the coats.
passages.ot:
Stephen saw what Daniel saw: one like a son of man before the Ancient of Days, “coming with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13), and the Lord at God's right hand, as Psalm 110 says: “Sit at My right hand” (Psalm 110:1).

The law of stoning is in Leviticus: “Take the blasphemer outside the camp” and “have the whole assembly stone him” (Leviticus 24:14), and in Deuteronomy: “The hands of the witnesses shall be the first in putting him to death” (Deuteronomy 17:7).
passages.hard:
Stephen dies as his Lord died. Jesus said, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit” (Luke 23:46); Stephen says, ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit’, praying to Jesus as Jesus prayed to the Father. Jesus prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34); Stephen prays, ‘Lord, do not hold this sin against them’. The first person to die for Jesus dies forgiving.

That prayer was answered in a way no one there could have guessed. The young man holding the coats became the apostle Paul. Years later he wrote, “I persecuted the church of God” (1 Corinthians 15:9), and, “I was shown mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13).

‘He fell asleep’ is the Bible's gentle word for the death of a believer. It does not hide the violence. It says that death does not have the last word.

A word for anyone who has lost someone to violence, or who has watched someone they love suffer. Stephen's death is told plainly, and so is his peace. Grief at such a loss is not a lack of faith. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a grief counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Stephen saw heaven open while the stones were falling, and he prayed for the people throwing them. Ask whom you most need to forgive, and whether you could pray, as he did, that their sin not be held against them. And remember Saul. The person you least expect may be the one God is about to call.
